title: Wave Interference — Superposition
concept: Superposition and the phase condition for interference
prompt: Two waves share one axis. Predict how they combine, then set a phase to cancel them.
learning_objective: Predict whether two waves interfere constructively, destructively or partially, and set a phase difference of 180 degrees to cancel a wave.
reference: PhET Wave Interference; ExploreLearning Gizmos Wave Superposition

spec.title: Wave Interference — Superposition
spec.instruction: Predict how the two waves combine, then set a phase to cancel them. The sum is computed point by point.

challenges.text: Wave A and wave B are identical and both have phase 0. Predict how they combine.
challenges.why: Equal waves with a phase difference of 0 degrees are in step: every crest lines up with a crest, so the displacements add and the peak doubles.

challenges.text: Wave B is now 180 degrees out of step with wave A. Predict how they combine.
challenges.why: A phase difference of 180 degrees is half a cycle: a crest of one meets a trough of the other, so the displacements cancel everywhere.

challenges.text: Wave B is 90 degrees out of step. Predict how they combine.
challenges.why: 90 degrees is neither in step nor out of step, so the waves partly reinforce and partly cancel. The resultant amplitude is sqrt(A1^2 + A2^2) here, not A1 + A2.

challenges.text: The two waves now have different wavelengths (4 m and 6 m) and the same phase. Predict how they combine.
challenges.why: With different wavelengths the phase difference grows along the axis, so the waves drift in and out of step and produce beats: reinforcement at some distances, cancellation at others.

challenges.text: Two equal waves, wave A fixed at phase 0. Set the phase of wave B so the two waves cancel.
challenges.why: Cancellation needs the waves half a cycle apart, so the phase difference must be 180 degrees (or an odd multiple of it).

challenges.text: Now set the phase of wave B so the two waves reinforce as strongly as possible.
challenges.why: Maximum reinforcement needs the waves in step, so the phase difference must be a whole number of cycles (0 degrees).

title: Wave Cancellation — Beats and Phasing
concept: Interference conditions with unequal amplitudes and wavelengths
prompt: Play with amplitude, wavelength and phase, then predict or set the interference condition.
learning_objective: Apply the phase condition for interference, including the residual amplitude left when amplitudes are unequal.
reference: PhET Wave Interference; standard superposition treatment

spec.title: Wave Cancellation — Beats and Phasing
spec.instruction: Explore the sliders, then answer each task. Remember: in step means a phase difference of 0 degrees, out of step means 180 degrees.

challenges.text: Free play. Move any slider and watch the red sum change.
Both waves have amplitude 2 and wavelength 6 m, and wave A has phase 0. Set wave B's phase so the waves cancel.
challenges.why: The wavelengths match and the amplitudes match, so a phase difference of 180 degrees gives complete cancellation.

challenges.text: Wave A has amplitude 1, wave B has amplitude 2, the wavelengths match, and the phases differ by 180 degrees. Predict how they combine.
challenges.why: A phase difference of 180 degrees is destructive interference whatever the amplitudes; because the amplitudes differ, the cancellation is only partial, leaving a residual amplitude of |2 - 1| = 1.

challenges.text: Same amplitudes (1 and 2), same wavelength, but now the phases differ by 90 degrees. Predict how they combine.
challenges.why: 90 degrees is a partial case: the resultant amplitude is sqrt(1^2 + 2^2) = sqrt(5) = 2.24, between |2 - 1| = 1 and 1 + 2 = 3.

challenges.text: Both waves have amplitude 1.5, wavelength 3 m, and wave A has phase 30 degrees. Set wave B's phase so the waves reinforce as strongly as possible.
challenges.why: Reinforcement needs the waves in step, so wave B must share wave A's phase: 30 degrees, or any phase that differs from it by a whole number of cycles.

title: Projectile Motion — Predicting the Range
concept: Projectile range R = v^2 sin(2 theta) / g
prompt: Explore the launch, then predict the range before you see the arc.
learning_objective: Compute a projectile's range from its launch speed and angle using R = v^2 sin(2 theta)/g, and identify complementary angles with equal range.

spec.title: Projectile Motion — Predicting the Range
spec.instruction: Play with the launch angle and speed, then answer each task. Take g = 9.81 m/s^2.

challenges.text: Free play. Set the angle and speed, then watch the arc with its apex, range and time of flight.
A ball is launched at 30 degrees with a speed of 24 m/s. Predict its range, in metres, before checking.
A ball is launched at 25 degrees with a speed of 22 m/s. Which of these other angles gives the same range at the same speed?
challenges.why: 25 + 65 = 90, and sin(2 theta) = sin(180 - 2 theta), so complementary angles give the same range.

challenges.text: Now a ball is launched at 60 degrees with a speed of 18 m/s. Predict its range, in metres.
challenges.why: sin(2 x 60) = sin 120 = 0.866, so R = 18^2 x 0.866 / 9.81 = 28.6 m. Note this is lower than 45 degrees at the same speed.

title: Projectile Motion — Complementary Angles
concept: Complementary launch angles and the maximum range at 45 degrees
prompt: Predict the range and find the angle that matches it.
learning_objective: Relate launch angle to range and explain why 45 degrees gives the greatest range for a given speed.

spec.title: Projectile Motion — Complementary Angles
spec.instruction: Explore the arc, then predict ranges and match angles. Take g = 9.81 m/s^2.

challenges.text: Free play. Try 30 degrees and 60 degrees at the same speed and compare the ranges.
A ball is launched at 45 degrees with a speed of 30 m/s. Predict its range, in metres.
challenges.why: At 45 degrees sin(2 theta) = 1, its largest value, so R = v^2/g = 900/9.81 = 91.7 m. That is the maximum range for this speed.

challenges.text: A ball is launched at 35 degrees with a speed of 26 m/s. Which of these other angles gives the same range at the same speed?
challenges.why: 35 + 55 = 90. Complementary angles have the same sin(2 theta), so they give equal ranges; the 55 degree launch is slower to rise but travels further horizontally.

title: Monohybrid Cross — Dominant and Recessive
concept: Monohybrid inheritance and the 3:1 phenotype ratio
prompt: Cross two parents and read the offspring genotypes and phenotype ratio.
learning_objective: Derive the phenotype ratio of a monohybrid cross from the Punnett square, and find the probability of a given genotype.
reference: ExploreLearning Gizmos Mouse Genetics; standard Mendelian genetics

spec.title: Monohybrid Cross — Dominant and Recessive
spec.instruction: The square and the ratio are built from the two parents. Predict before you check.

challenges.text: Cross two heterozygous purple plants, Pp x Pp. Predict the phenotype ratio of the offspring.
challenges.why: Each parent makes P and p gametes, so the square is 3 purple (PP, Pp, Pp) to 1 white (pp).

challenges.text: From the cross Pp x Pp, what is the probability that an offspring is homozygous recessive (pp) and so has white flowers?
challenges.why: Exactly one of the four equally likely squares is pp, so the probability is 1/4.

challenges.text: Now cross a heterozygous plant with a white-flowered plant, Pp x pp. Predict the phenotype ratio.
challenges.why: Pp makes P and p gametes while pp makes only p, so half the offspring are purple (Pp) and half white (pp): 1:1.

challenges.text: Choose two parent genotypes whose cross gives a 3:1 ratio of purple to white flowers.
challenges.why: Two heterozygotes, Pp x Pp, give 3 purple to 1 white. Crossing a heterozygote with a homozygous dominant (PP x Pp) gives all purple, and Pp x pp gives 1:1.

title: Dihybrid Cross — Independent Assortment
prompt: Cross two parents for two traits and read the four-phenotype ratio.
learning_objective: Derive the phenotype ratio of a dihybrid cross, and the probability of a specific two-trait genotype.
reference: ExploreLearning Gizmos Chicken Genetics; standard Mendelian genetics

spec.title: Dihybrid Cross — Independent Assortment
spec.instruction: Two traits: seed shape (R/r) and seed colour (Y/y). The square is built from the parents you set.

challenges.text: Cross two plants heterozygous for both traits, RrYy x RrYy. Predict the phenotype ratio.
challenges.why: Each parent makes four gamete types (RY, Ry, rY, ry), so the 4 x 4 square gives 9 round-yellow : 3 round-green : 3 wrinkled-yellow : 1 wrinkled-green.

challenges.text: From RrYy x RrYy, what is the probability that an offspring is rryy (wrinkled and green)?
challenges.why: Only one of the sixteen squares is rryy, so the probability is 1/16. Each recessive trait on its own is 1/4, and 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16.

challenges.text: Now cross a double heterozygote with a double recessive, RrYy x rryy. Predict the phenotype ratio.
challenges.why: This is a test cross: the rryy parent contributes only recessive alleles, so the four gametes of RrYy show up directly as four equally likely phenotypes, 1:1:1:1.

challenges.text: Choose two parents whose cross gives a 1:1:1:1 ratio across the four phenotypes.
challenges.why: A double heterozygote crossed with a double recessive (RrYy x rryy) gives 1:1:1:1. Crossing two double heterozygotes gives 9:3:3:1 instead.

title: Incomplete Dominance — Blending
concept: Incomplete dominance and the 1:2:1 phenotype ratio
prompt: Cross two pink-flowered plants and read the ratio of the three phenotypes.
learning_objective: Explain why incomplete dominance gives a 1:2:1 phenotype ratio rather than 3:1.

spec.title: Incomplete Dominance — Blending
spec.instruction: Red (RR) crossed with white (WW) gives pink (RW). Work out the ratio from the square.

challenges.text: Cross two pink-flowered plants, RW x RW. Predict the phenotype ratio of the offspring.
challenges.why: The heterozygote has its own phenotype, so the ratio of red : pink : white follows the genotypes 1:2:1, not the 3:1 of complete dominance.

challenges.text: From RW x RW, what is the probability that an offspring is heterozygous (RW) and so pink?
challenges.why: Two of the four squares are RW, so the probability is 2/4 = 1/2. The heterozygote is the most common outcome.

challenges.text: Choose two parent genotypes whose cross gives a 1:2:1 ratio of red to pink to white flowers.
challenges.why: Two pink plants, RW x RW, give 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. Red x white gives all pink, and pink x white gives 1 pink : 1 white.

title: Gravity and Orbits — The Escape Speed
concept: Orbital energy and the escape speed sqrt(2GM/r)
prompt: Launch a satellite and predict whether it orbits, crashes or escapes.
learning_objective: Classify a satellite's fate from its launch speed relative to the escape speed, and find the speed for a circular orbit.
reference: PhET Gravity and Orbits; standard orbital mechanics

spec.title: Gravity and Orbits — The Escape Speed
spec.instruction: Predict the fate of the satellite, then check by running the orbit. The escape speed is sqrt(2GM/r).

challenges.text: Free play. Set the central mass and the launch speed, then watch the orbit.
Central mass 5.97 x 10^24 kg (Earth). The satellite is launched at 12.0 km/s. Predict its fate.
challenges.why: The escape speed at this radius is 10.67 km/s. At 12.0 km/s the total energy is positive, so the satellite is unbound and escapes.

challenges.text: Same central mass, but the satellite is launched at only 7.0 km/s. Predict its fate.
challenges.why: The circular speed is 7.55 km/s. At 7.0 km/s the launch point is the apoapsis and the periapsis falls below the surface, so the orbit hits the body.

challenges.text: Same central mass, launched at 9.5 km/s. Predict its fate.
challenges.why: 9.5 km/s is above the circular speed of 7.55 km/s but below the escape speed of 10.67 km/s, so the orbit is a bound ellipse that stays clear of the body.

challenges.text: Central mass 5.97 x 10^24 kg. Find the launch speed that gives a circular orbit (within 3%).
challenges.why: A circular orbit needs the speed sqrt(GM/r) = 7.55 km/s, where gravity supplies exactly the required centripetal acceleration.

challenges.text: Now the central mass is 12 x 10^24 kg. Find a launch speed that escapes.
challenges.why: With a heavier body the escape speed rises to sqrt(2GM/r) = 15.1 km/s, so you need a much higher launch speed than for Earth.

title: Orbits and Mass — How Speed Sets the Path
concept: Circular speed and escape speed scale with the central mass
prompt: Change the central mass and predict how the orbit changes.
learning_objective: Predict how the circular and escape speeds depend on the central mass, and classify orbits across masses.
reference: PhET Gravity and Orbits; standard orbital mechanics

spec.title: Orbits and Mass — How Speed Sets the Path
spec.instruction: The escape speed grows with the square root of the central mass. Predict each fate, then check.

challenges.text: Free play. Halve the mass and see what happens to the escape speed.
Central mass 2 x 10^24 kg. The satellite is launched at 5.0 km/s. Predict its fate.
challenges.why: For this lighter body the circular speed is 4.37 km/s and the escape speed is 6.18 km/s. At 5.0 km/s the orbit is bound and clear of the body.

challenges.text: Same light body (2 x 10^24 kg), but launched at 7.0 km/s. Predict its fate.
challenges.why: The escape speed is only 6.18 km/s here, so 7.0 km/s is above it and the satellite escapes.

challenges.text: Now a heavy body, 10 x 10^24 kg, launched at 6.0 km/s. Predict its fate.
challenges.why: The circular speed is 9.76 km/s, so 6.0 km/s is far too slow: the satellite is bound but its periapsis falls inside the body and it crashes.
